title: E41 - The Future of AI is People: Legal Quants Founders Jamie Tso & Raymond Sun
author: Jamie Tso · Raymond Sun

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not substantively address the cluster’s central claim that automation threatens apprenticeship and future verification capacity. Instead, it reframes AI as a learning aid and recommends practical experimentation on understood workflow problems, shifting the emphasis from reconstructing threatened training systems to people-led adoption and service redesign.

kp.k: Accelerating AI makes continuous experimentation increasingly important
kp.d: Tso and Sun describe difficulty keeping pace with AI, with Sun locating a marked acceleration since DeepSeek in 2025. Abramowitz argues that early adoption compounds not only practical capability but readiness to understand new possibilities. Tso recommends experimenting with accessible frontier technology to develop AI literacy. These are practitioner experiences and recommendations, not measured adoption findings.
qs: I feel that I have never felt so behind in AI.
Every two weeks, there's something that's come out, and each week replaces the development of the previous week.
the value of early adoption is compounding, not just in your capabilities and knowing like what prompts to push, but just what your brain is ready to wrap itself around

kp.k: AI could redesign legal delivery, not merely improve efficiency
kp.d: Sun frames lawyers as translators between legal language and society, historically performing information-heavy work manually. He proposes moving beyond efficiency improvements toward legal requirements embedded in clients' products and services and made directly operational. This is a prospective service-design argument, rather than evidence of completed transformation.
qs: Fundamentally, lawyers have been the bridge between the law and broader society.

How do we not only use AI to help make our existing processes efficient, but also getting ourselves out of the box and really redefining how legal is delivered to the broader society and make it even more useful to clients, right?
having legal requirements, for example, be more directly operationalizable and more embedded within whatever product or service that the client is trying to get your advice on.

kp.k: Lawyer-built software changes the build-versus-buy calculation
kp.d: Abramowitz contrasts historically problematic firm-IT development with end users now building tools tailored to their own workflows and rebuilding them when needs change. Sun calls this a new layer of highly personalized, potentially single-use software. Abramowitz's deal-specific data room is a hypothetical illustration, not a reported deployment.
qs: I think we're talking about like the actual users who can build this for themselves, tailored.
if their workflow changes, they can literally throw it out and start from scratch and rebuild it
Here we're now at this point in time where you can create a very hyper-personalized software, and it can just be for one time use.

kp.k: Vibe coding develops skills beyond the resulting applications
kp.d: Tso argues that the principal value of lawyer-built applications is the underlying technical capability: understanding systems, diagnosing failures, and iterating on workflows. He contrasts this with off-the-shelf tools that he characterizes as opaque and difficult for users to fix. His account treats building as an unusually intensive form of AI literacy rather than simply cheaper software procurement.
qs: we're looking at the skills of these lawyers rather than the apps that they built.
It's an extreme form of AI literacy.
you kind of have that quick iterative loop where you can test, iterate, and design your own workflows, apps, and skills.

kp.k: Security and production readiness remain acknowledged objections
kp.d: Tso acknowledges objections that vibe-coded applications are insecure or not production-ready, but predicts cloud providers will solve these problems. Abramowitz argues that excessive guardrails can encourage use of personal AI and suggests bespoke tools need not meet one-to-many scalability requirements. Neither speaker supplies security testing or deployment evidence; Abramowitz ultimately distinguishes experimentation from production use for clients.
qs: the tools themselves are not production ready. You know, the apps are not secure.
Of course, these are important problems. But I think that will be solved down the road by the cloud providers.
if you're going to give me like lame AI at work, I'm going to use my own AI.
I'm not telling you to productionize it for a client yet, but just kind of get going and get learning.

kp.k: Vendor differentiation may shift from interfaces to infrastructure
kp.d: Sun predicts that customers' ability to build bespoke interfaces will challenge interface-focused vendors. Looking three to five years ahead, he argues that defensible value may instead lie in underlying reasoning capabilities and infrastructure on which custom applications depend. Abramowitz cites Sandstone's legal-department data-integration thesis as an example and discloses his investment in the company.
qs: if the customer can solve their own problem through these tools, they solve the interface problem, that really is a challenge for a lot of the interface specific vendors.
if in three to five years time, we know that our own customers are building the most bespoke interfaces and we can't compete with them on that front
I feel like a lot of the modes will now become an infrastructural battle, less so an app layer battle
I just invested in a company called Sandstone

kp.k: Human trust remains central to high-value legal services
kp.d: Tso predicts that AI will underpin legal services while the client-facing interface remains human, especially for consequential transactions. His $5 billion merger example rests on the importance of interpersonal trust. He expresses skepticism about AI-to-AI negotiation calls as a productive substitute; this is a judgment about future delivery, not comparative performance evidence.
qs: lawyering is a people business. There's a lot of soft skill.
If you're doing a $5 billion merger, then you better talk to a lawyer, a human, because I think that's how we build trust.
a lot of things would be AI enabled at a fundamental layer, but that's still interface, the interface would still be human.

kp.k: Community and talent may outlast software-based competitive advantages
kp.d: Abramowitz argues that user communities could become a major source of software-company value. Tso agrees, predicting software costs approach zero while talent remains valuable, and describes LegalQuants as a vehicle to discover, showcase, and upskill lawyer-builders. He reports growth from five WhatsApp participants to around 100, with hundreds of daily messages and rapid sharing of technology tests. These figures are founder-reported community activity, not independent evidence of commercial success.
qs: the future of valuable software ironically is in community.
The software cost is going to zero. But talents aren't, right?
The whole mission of legal quants is to highlight the talents.
It started with just five people. Then it slowly grew. Now it's around 100 people. We have hundreds of messages per day

kp.k: Law firms should strengthen client-facing human experiences
kp.d: Abramowitz recommends repurposing law-firm offices to attract clients through valuable collaboration and meeting experiences, arguing that lawyers would then want to attend. He links this proposal to his prediction that software development and document creation costs will approach zero, requiring firms to reconsider where value resides. This is the host's strategic suggestion, not a guest finding or demonstrated return-to-office intervention.
qs: You build your office to attract clients.
What would make our clients want to come into our office and see massive value in doing that regularly?
I think we probably at some point say document creation probably goes to zero.

kp.k: Proactive legal systems could unlock previously unused client rights
kp.d: Tso offers a hypothetical funds-law service for institutional investors holding a thousand side letters whose negotiated rights are difficult for the GC to track. He proposes AI screening them daily, identifying exercisable rights, and automatically notifying the general partner. He presents this as new client intelligence and a source of differentiation rather than routine document-production efficiency; no implemented system or results are reported.
qs: They've gathered like a thousand different side letters.
Maybe there is some notification rights that they're entitled to. Maybe there are some audit rights that, you know, they can actually exercise.
I'll basically build them an AI that would just screen your side letters daily
automatically send a notification to the GP asking for them to be respected.

kp.k: Distinctive AI-enabled services could support exceptional pricing
kp.d: Abramowitz suggests that charging $10,000 an hour could become plausible when an hour produces a proactive system rather than a document. Tso attributes potential pricing power to scarce expertise and the absence of comparable services, while acknowledging that copying would require continuing innovation. This is a speculative pricing argument, not evidence of actual rates or a prediction that hourly billing necessarily disappears.
qs: this is where the prediction that lawyers might soon charge $10,000 an hour is not so crazy, right?
the reason why they can charge that amount is there is no comparable in the market.
once that kind of service appears in the market, people will try to copy

kp.k: Legal quants own strategy rather than merely implement tools
kp.d: The guests distinguish their proposed legal-quant role from implementation-focused legal engineering: originating service ideas and owning a strategy rather than simply coding to instructions. Sun grounds his comparison in his own 2017 legal-engineering experience. Tso analogizes future rainmakers to portfolio managers responsible for strategies and client niches, predicting that strong technological understanding will enable new service markets. The distinction is their proposed role framework, not a documented profession-wide occupational classification.
qs: A legal engineer is given a task, a plan to execute.
I just followed the instructions of the PM, I coded it and that's it.
Legal quants, that's completely different, right?
you have the idea and then you try to, whether it's AI implementing for you or others helping you implement, regardless of what, it's the idea, right?

kp.k: Legal value could shift from labor to enterprise
kp.d: Sun uses the economic factors of production—land, labor, capital, and enterprise—to argue that legal services should move beyond pricing time and effort toward combining resources into a service. He sees this question spanning solo practitioners, boutiques, large firms, and legal-tech vendors. Abramowitz adds that lawyers can now pursue entrepreneurial projects without leaving legal practice. These are conceptual arguments about value creation, not measured business-model changes.
qs: our economics has been based on the four factors of production, land, labor, capital, enterprise.
X time equals X dollars, right? X effort equals X dollars.
your value is coming from the fact that you combine the other factors of production together to create a service
you don't have to leave law to do something like exciting and entrepreneurial and new.

kp.k: Existing career structures may underuse hybrid legal talent
kp.d: Tso reports conversations with lawyer-builders who struggle to find supportive spaces in traditional firms and find startup roles insufficiently exciting. He characterizes this as talent misallocation and argues for infrastructure and opportunities enabling technically capable legal generalists to contribute more effectively. His claim is based on unspecified practitioner conversations, not a quantified labor-market study.
qs: Their common frustration is that, well, they don't seem to have been able to find that space.
the offers that came back, or the roles that they're being given, are also not that exciting.
This is like a talent problem of our industry.

kp.k: Code, content, and community form complementary productive assets
kp.d: Sun proposes a three-Cs framework in which technology, content, and an ecosystem reinforce one another in future small businesses and personal brands. He treats these as alternative forms of capital as tools become more accessible and money becomes less of a barrier. In the episode this is a cross-domain conceptual framework informing LegalQuants, not empirical evidence that all successful legal businesses require these elements.
qs: the three C's theory, which stands for code, content and community.
code, which represents the tech and also community, which represents the ecosystem.
these three Cs become the new definition of capital.

kp.k: AI dispute resolution raises concrete governance questions
kp.d: Abramowitz reports that the American Arbitration Association has built an AI arbitrator for a narrowly defined, documents-only construction-dispute use case and discloses that his business works with it. He says the EU AI Act imposes greater governance and disclosure concerns around judicial and dispute-resolution decisions. Separately, he floats a very broad possible reading encompassing lawyers' contract drafting; this is explicitly hypothetical interpretation, not an established legal holding or a guest-endorsed rule.
qs: We work with the American Arbitration Association that has built the first AI arbitrator for a very limited set of use cases.
you could theoretically say that drafting a contract at some point is meant to influence a judge if that contract then becomes the subject of a dispute.
There's more governance and disclosures, you know, required around doing it.

kp.k: Training should prioritize concrete problems, iteration, and initiative
kp.d: Sun recommends solving a personally frustrating work problem too bespoke or uncommercial for vendors, using lawyers' research skills to identify inputs, outputs, and possible solutions. Tso emphasizes motivation and persistence through buggy tools, reporting high personal agency among legal quants he has met over the past two months. Here agency means human initiative, not autonomous AI agents. The recommendations privilege applied experimentation over learning theory without application.
qs: I feel like application is the most important thing.
think about one thing that's really annoying in your work.
those really personal, custom problems that you really, that you really dread and it makes your job boring. Focus on that
for the legal quants that I've met for the past two months, all of them have extremely high agency.
you kind of need to have that kind of motivation and that kind of grit to tolerate the buckiness of whatever AI tool that they are using.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Tso and Sun predict a shift from lawyers consuming standard software to lawyers building bespoke tools and technology-enabled legal services, with competitive value increasingly residing in human capabilities, infrastructure and communities.
pts.d: Raymond Sun (00:13:38) argues that AI can change not only the efficiency of existing work but also how legal services are delivered, including embedding operational legal requirements in clients' products and services. Jamie Tso (00:20:47) describes lawyer-built applications as evidence of deeper AI literacy: configuring systems allows lawyers to test, diagnose and iterate rather than depend on an off-the-shelf black box. Sun (00:24:45–00:25:57) identifies an emerging category of hyper-personalised, potentially single-use software. He predicts that customers' ability to build their own interfaces will challenge interface-focused vendors, shifting competitive differentiation towards underlying models and infrastructure. Tso (00:29:24–00:30:33) expects human relationships and trust to remain central, especially in major transactions, notwithstanding AI-enabled underlying work; he is sceptical that simulated AI-to-AI negotiation calls would be productive. Tso (00:33:20) predicts software costs approaching zero while talent retains value, and argues that technological excellence will become part of legal excellence. Tso (00:41:56) proposes, rather than reports deploying, a service that continuously screens institutional investors' side letters, identifies exercisable rights and sends notifications to fund managers. He argues that lawyers' imagination and knowledge of client interests are essential to inventing such services. In responding to a hypothetical high hourly price introduced by the interviewer, Tso (00:44:45) attributes possible premium pricing to scarce capabilities and an absence of comparable services; he expects imitation to drive continuing innovation. Tso (00:48:39) predicts that future rainmakers will use technology to create new ways of serving clients and new markets. Sun (00:49:52) frames the economic change as a move from charging for labour towards entrepreneurial combination of resources. He distinguishes the strategic, idea-owning legal quant from the implementation-focused legal-engineer role he previously held. Tso (00:53:55) expects technically capable generalists to succeed but identifies a current mismatch between their capabilities and available jobs. Both speakers recommend learning through execution on concrete work problems; Tso (01:11:32) regards personal initiative and persistence as important determinants of effective AI use.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The speakers primarily offer first-hand professional and community experience, illustrative scenarios and economic reasoning, rather than measured legal-service outcomes.
pts.d: Tso supports the lawyer-developer and talent thesis with his own experimentation and observations of LegalQuants, reporting growth from five members to around 100 and hundreds of daily messages about frontier technology. Sun points to the community's combined legal, technical and regulatory capabilities. Their community observations are self-reported and concern a selected, invitation-only group; they are not a representative study of lawyers. Tso's side-letter example draws on his experience as a funds lawyer but is phrased as a proposed service, not a documented deployment or measured client benefit. His pricing argument rests on scarcity, demand and subsequent imitation, informed partly by his finance interests and completion of the CFA programme's three levels. Sun's distinction between implementation and strategic ownership draws on his own legal-engineer work beginning in 2017. Tso reports conversations with technically capable lawyers who find existing firms and startup jobs insufficiently accommodating, and reports high personal initiative among legal quants he met over the preceding two months. No named benchmark, controlled comparison, legal-service productivity dataset, realised fee evidence or security evaluation is supplied for these predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Bespoke tool-building is presented as already possible in the 2026 conversation; broader market and professional changes are conditional forecasts, with a three-to-five-year horizon for customers displacing vendor interfaces.
pts.d: Sun presents custom software as a current capability, while suggesting that reinvented service delivery follows lawyers becoming accustomed to AI-assisted work. His infrastructure prediction explicitly considers customers building superior bespoke interfaces in three to five years; vendors can retain relevance if those applications still require their underlying capabilities. Tso acknowledges that lawyer-built tools may not yet be secure or production-ready and predicts that cloud providers will address those problems later, without a deadline or demonstrated solution. His human-interface argument is particularly grounded in high-value, trust-sensitive transactions, not a claim that every task must remain manual. At 00:33:20 he treats today's coding skills as a moving target: agent design might be a year away but, he immediately qualifies, should happen much sooner. Premium pricing depends on a lawyer offering a credible service without comparable alternatives; imitation makes the advantage temporary and requires continued innovation. No precise date is supplied for near-zero software costs, the reallocation of professional value or the rise of technology-enabled rainmakers. Tso's recommendations depend on motivation and tolerance of buggy tools; Sun recommends beginning with a personally understood problem too specialised to attract commercial vendors. Their emphasis on personal agency is about human initiative, not a forecast that autonomous AI agents will perform all legal work.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect practising lawyers, firms of all sizes, software vendors and corporate clients, with particular advantages claimed for lawyers combining legal judgment, technical capability and entrepreneurial initiative.
pts.d: Practising lawyers could solve individual workflow problems themselves and create new services instead of merely using purchased tools. LegalQuants is presented as a community for discovering, developing and showcasing that combined talent, not as an established alternative legal service provider. Technically capable lawyers may face poor organisational fit in traditional firms or existing startup roles. Sun extends the shift from labour-based value to entrepreneurial service creation across individual practices, boutiques, large firms and legal-tech vendors. Interface-focused vendors face customer self-build competition; model and infrastructure providers could remain necessary suppliers. Large institutional investors and their general counsel are the specific intended beneficiaries of Tso's proposed side-letter monitoring service, which would help operationalise contractual rights otherwise difficult to track. Major-transaction clients would continue to rely on human trust and relationships under Tso's forecast. Future partners and rainmakers could differentiate themselves by developing technology-enabled services and markets. The discussion of broader societal delivery does not provide a concrete prediction about closing the civil justice gap or quantify benefits to underserved individuals.
